messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Project Manager
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Cold Temperature: Cold, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
  Maladaptive Strategies: Memory Erasure: I try to erase the memory of the event, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life, Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 42, Linh Tran described the illness that nearly killed her as something that still did not feel entirely like her own life. She was a married Vietnamese American woman working as a project manager, used to deadlines, spreadsheets, and the steady competence of being the person others relied on. The medical crisis interrupted that identity abruptly. She recalled becoming critically ill and being rushed into intensive treatment, where much of her experience narrowed to fragments: the sting and sight of needles entering her skin, clear bags hanging from metal poles, tubing, antiseptic smells, and the cold that seemed to live everywhere in the hospital. Even now, when she tried to tell the story from beginning to end, she could only do it in pieces. Some moments were sharply preserved—the glint of a needle, the sight of a drip chamber, the sterile chemical smell in the room, the cold air against her skin—while other stretches were blank. She would stop in session and say that the whole thing sounded too extreme to have really happened to her, as if she were describing another woman’s catastrophe.

In the weeks after she survived and returned home, Linh expected gratitude and relief, but what stood out instead was how often the emotional force of the illness arrived without warning. At times she would suddenly feel the same terror and helplessness she remembered from the hospital, yet have no picture in her mind to go with it. The feeling would surge through her body before she could place it. At other times a specific image would snap into focus with uncomfortable clarity: a needle, a bag of fluid, the clinical brightness of the room. She had begun to believe that something about the experience had damaged her not only physically but fundamentally. She was certain her body had been permanently weakened. Ordinary sensations were hard for her to trust. If she felt tired, chilled, or slightly unwell, her mind went quickly to the conviction that the illness had changed her for good.

Linh also spoke with anguish about having failed in what she saw as her most important role. Before the illness, she had taken pride in being dependable at home and at work. During the medical crisis she had needed care from her husband and others, and afterward she could not stop measuring herself against the version of herself who had managed everything. She had come to see the episode as proof that her life had been destroyed in some essential way. She still went to work, but the world of work had become crowded with reminders she had not anticipated. As a project manager, she spent much of her day in a heavily air-conditioned office where the sudden chill on her arms could bring her back to the hospital at once. Delivery staff sometimes passed through with disinfectant on their hands, and the smell was enough to make her stomach drop. When colleagues discussed a health issue or someone returned from a medical appointment with a bandage, Linh found herself looking away quickly, her mind already filling with the sight of drips and needles.

Over months, she developed rigid ways of trying to keep herself together. She tried to erase the memory whenever it surfaced, cutting off images, changing the subject in her own mind, telling herself not to go there. She watched her thoughts closely, scanning for any sign that she was losing control or “going crazy.” If a wave of fear came over her without an image attached, that frightened her especially; she took the sheer intensity of feeling as evidence that her mind was no longer reliable. Medical settings became particularly difficult. She avoided hospitals, would not go near ambulances if she could help it, and postponed physical examinations. Even routine checkups felt impossible because the sight of medical equipment, especially needles or IV drips, seemed too close to the moments she remembered most clearly. What looked to others like simple avoidance made sense to Linh as self-protection: she was trying to prevent herself from being overwhelmed, from confirming her fear that her body was damaged beyond repair, and from facing a story she still could barely believe belonged to her.

These habits began to narrow her life. At work she quietly delegated tasks that might take her near the building’s first-aid station and made excuses when wellness events were held onsite. At home, her husband urged her to follow up medically, but their conversations often ended in tension because Linh felt he could not understand how impossible it was to walk back into anything resembling that world. By the time she sought help, she was exhausted by the effort of policing her mind and arranging her life around reminders of illness. What finally brought her in was the recognition that she could no longer separate fear of medical cues from fear of herself—fear of what might happen if she remembered too much, and fear of what it meant that so much remained blank. More than anything, she wanted some way to live in her body without feeling that the worst had already happened and would somehow happen again.
